nodes.label: Per-Method Wall-Clock Timeout (180s default)
nodes.rationale: Heavy methods (SPPR_EwE path enumeration, Monte-Carlo drivers) can run for hours and cannot be interrupted once inside numpy/sympy, so each method runs in a worker process with a wall-clock budget; an overrun is killed, recorded as a timeout (not a failure) in run_notes' status column, and the export moves on to the next method. One shared worker keeps the cost to a single process spawn per directory rather than per model.

nodes.label: Nullspace Fixed-Point Formulation (x = A·x, nullspace of L = A − I)
nodes.rationale: The SPPR vector is a fixed point of the per-edge weight matrix A (eigenvalue 1), so it lives in the nullspace of L = A − I; solving in closed form automatically sums all pathways and all cycles (the geometric series I + A + A² + …), which path enumeration struggles to do exactly.
nodes.norm_label: nullspace fixed-point formulation (x = a·x, nullspace of l = a − i)

nodes.label: Detritus Recycling Coupled System ((I − B)x = c)
nodes.rationale: Detritus is not a true primary source: its SPPR value depends on the SPPR of everything dying into it, which itself depends partly on detritus's own value, producing a self-consistency fixed point. With multiple pools this becomes a linear system (I−B)x=c, where B is the recycling coupling traced through the living nullspace and back down through mortality/egestion; solved because a single scalar or matrix solve closes the death→detritus→consumption→death loop exactly rather than approximating it.
nodes.norm_label: detritus recycling coupled system ((i − b)x = c)

nodes.label: Spectral Radius Convergence Condition (b = ρ(B) < 1, Perron–Frobenius)
nodes.rationale: B is entrywise non-negative, so by Perron–Frobenius (I−B)⁻¹ ≥ 0 iff b < 1: only then is a finite non-negative solution guaranteed for every admissible c. b ≥ 1 means recycling regenerates at least as much detritus as it consumes each pass, so the Neumann series diverges; this is why det_collapse_mode offers 'auto'/'always' pooling as a stabilizing fallback rather than trusting the direct solve unconditionally.
nodes.norm_label: spectral radius convergence condition (b = ρ(b) < 1, perron–frobenius)

nodes.label: monte_carlo_SPPR Jensen's-Inequality Correction
nodes.rationale: SPPR is a function of 1/TE, which is convex, so by Jensen's inequality E[1/TE] ≥ 1/E[TE], hence E[SPPR(TE)] ≥ SPPR(E[TE]): solving once at the mean TE systematically underestimates expected PPR because it ignores the extra requirement contributed by the low-TE tail. monte_carlo_SPPR exists specifically to recover the unbiased (higher) expectation by resampling TE and averaging, not merely to produce an error bar.

nodes.label: Gamma-Distribution TE Resampling
nodes.rationale: TE must stay strictly positive because 1/TE diverges near zero and negative TE is meaningless, so each per-group TE is drawn from a Gamma(alpha, theta) distribution parameterized to preserve the model mean and a specified coefficient of variation — a symmetric normal would be wrong here. Non-positive model TEs are pinned rather than sampled, since gamma requires a strictly positive scale.

nodes.label: Group-Level Jensen-Affected PPR Aggregation (SeaAroundUs)
nodes.rationale: Commercial/functional group SPPR exponentiates the group's catch-weighted mean trophic level once, rather than summing each taxon's own exponentiated SPPR. Because SPPR = 10^(TL-1) is convex, this is a direct, deliberate application of Jensen's inequality: group PPR can only ever be ≤ the sum of its member taxa's PPR, never more. The gap is kept on purpose — it measures the cost of moving from taxa to groups, which an Ecopath model cannot show on its own because it has no taxon level. In this 2019 EEZ release the understatement is 22.27% for commercial groups and 14.44% for functional groups; the top-level repository README reports a related but distinct 'globally' measured figure of 22.93%/16.48%.
